title: Kramers' Theorem Leaves a Topological Footprint in Classical Records
abstract: Time reversal $Θ$ squares to $-1$ on a half-integer spin, so every state is orthogonal to its time reverse. This sign has been read only from quantum objects. The equilibrium state loses it, but the classical record keeps it. For a detector that resolves handedness, the probabilities that one stretch of record is followed by the time reverse of another measure the cohomology class of time reversal, $Θ^2=\pm1$. Their matrix carries this sign in its signature, a topological integer that survives equal emission and absorption losses. A programmed emitter on quantum processors reads it in about $10^3$ shots.
summary: This paper shows that the topological signature of time reversal ($\Theta^2$) can be extracted from classical measurement records of quantum systems. By analyzing the inertia of the probability kernel, the authors demonstrate that this signature is a robust invariant, allowing for a quantitative test of fundamental symmetries in open quantum systems.
main_problem: The paper investigates how the topological signature of time reversal ($\Theta^2 = \pm 1$) can be extracted from classical records generated by quantum measurements, even when the equilibrium state loses this information.
main_result: The signature of the probability matrix, derived from the kernel $K(x, y)$, is a robust topological invariant that survives losses and is determined by $\Theta^2$. For half-integer spin systems, this implies $\Theta^2 = -1$.
method: The analysis uses concepts from linear algebra, specifically Sylvester's law of inertia, applied to the kernel matrix $K(x, y)$ formed from measurement records, relating its signature to the time-reversal parity $\Theta^2$.
model_or_system: The model involves a monitored quantum spin exchanging quanta with a thermal bath, described by master equations and Kraus operators. The core diagnostic tool is the comparison between the probability of a record $x$ followed by its time reverse $	au(x)$ versus other sequences.
key_observables: The signature $(n_+, n_-)$ of the kernel matrix, the probability $P(x|x)$, and the cohomology class of time reversal, $\Theta^2$.
important_parameters: Half-integer spin (Kramers doublet) vs. integer spin; the number of measurement shots ($10^3$ to $10^{16}$); and the purity $	ext{Tr} \hat{ho}_x^2$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the detector resolves handedness (circular polarization) to measure the full topological signature, and that losses treat emission and absorption symmetrically.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the process of measuring $P(xy)$ and its dependence on $\Theta^2$. Figure 2 shows how the rescaled probability $rP(x|x)/P(x)$ depends on the spin value and detection method.
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the problem (measuring $\Theta^2$ classically) to deriving the mathematical framework using the kernel $K(x, y)$ and its inertia. It then applies this to quantum emitters, showing how the signature is robustly read out, even in the presence of noise.
why_interesting: This work bridges fundamental symmetries (time reversal) with measurable, topological quantities derived from open quantum system dynamics, providing a novel diagnostic tool for quantum hardware.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. (a) An equilibrium spin exchanges quanta with a bath at inverse temperature β. (b) A record and its time reverse across the time t. The time reverse reads the past backwards with emission and absorption exchanged. The past predicts a state ψ, and its time reverse retrodicts Θψ. (c) The probability of the pair is the overlap of ψ and Θψ [Eq. (2)] and vanishes for Θ2 = −1. The matrix of such probabilities has signature Θ2d [Eq. (5)].

FIG. 2. (a) Rescaled probability rP(x|x)/P(x) that a stretch x is followed by its time reverse, against the purity Tr ˆρ2 x of the state that x prepares, for stretches of up to four jumps (three for S = 5/2). Kramers emitters with S = 3/2 and 5/2 fall on the line 1 −Tr ˆρ2 x of Eq. (3). The programmed doublet with Θ2 = 1 lies between this line and the dotted line of slope one, and a non-degenerate level sits at 1. Under linear detection the Kramers pseudospin stays maximally mixed. (b) The four largest eigenvalues of one kernel block divided by the largest. The pairs above each group give the inertia (n+, n−). A tilted spin 3/2 gives (1, 3) under circular detection and (1, 0) under linear...

FIG. 3. (a) Probability that the protocol returns the full reading, (1, 3) for the programmed Kramers doublet and (3, 1) for its Θ2 = 1 control. Each point averages 60 simulated experiments, none of which returned the wrong class. Noisy runs add per step 3% readout error, 1% Pauli noise and 1% amplitude damping of the data qubit. (b) Estimated number of independent detected windows needed for the full reading of an equilibrium spin against the detection efficiency η of both emission and absorption. The two S = 3/2 curves are the most favorable of 12 random orientations of the splitting axes and a slower one. The dotted line marks the programmed emitter of panel (a).
